content.text:
A child who runs from the potty

The time to give up diapers has come, but your child shouts "No, I won't sit!" in front of the potty and runs away. Watching them glance around nervously after an accident, a parent's heart starts to race too.

But the more you rush potty training, the more tense your child becomes. What's needed here isn't pressure, but one warm story that tells them the potty isn't scary.

Curious about the potty training storybook plot? We take a look at the lessons of the potty training storybook alongside the illustrations. Meet the key scenes of the potty training storybook too. Read the potty training storybook together with your child and talk about the story. From how to potty train a child to a child scared of the potty and when to stop using diapers, we've gathered all kinds of stories about 04. Pee Goes In, Great Job!

content.alt: 04. Pee Goes In, Great Job! - Potty training moves at its own pace
content.text:
Potty training moves at its own pace

Potty training is a developmental process that moves at a different pace for every child. Some manage it quickly, some slowly, and the accidents along the way aren't mistakes but a natural part of learning.

What a child needs at this stage are two things: the reassurance that the potty isn't scary, and the ability to notice the tickly "I need to go" signal on their own. Let go of the hurry and follow your child's pace, and one day the moment comes when they run to the toilet all by themselves.
content.caption: They learn that a tickly tummy is the signal to go.

content.alt: 04. Pee Goes In, Great Job! - Hoya's first potty success story
content.text:
Hoya's first potty success story

Baby Hoya, the hero of Pee Goes In, Great Job!, is scared of the potty at first and runs away. Then Mom scoops Hoya up in a hug and says, "You don't have to do it all at once, just a little at a time, one step at a time!"

Just sitting on the potty for a moment earns clapping cheers from Mom and big brother Hori. Hoya learns to feel the tickly signal too, and before long toddles over to the potty and finally succeeds. "I did it all by myself!" Hoya's shoulders puff up with pride.
content.caption: A little at a time, one step at a time, and finally I did it all by myself!

content.alt: 04. Pee Goes In, Great Job! - Gentle potty training at home
content.text:
Gentle potty training at home

Once you've read the story, it's time to carry it into practice at home. Here are a few ideas.

First, praise even the small successes generously. Recognizing loudly even just sitting on the potty or saying the signal gives your child a sense of achievement. Second, move forward a little at a time, one step at a time. Don't hurry; just follow your child's pace. Third, reassure them that accidents are okay. The words "we're all growing up little by little" ease the tension.
content.caption: A little at a time, one step at a time, follow your child's pace.

content.text:
Frequently Asked Questions

Q. When should potty training start?

A. A good sign to start is when your child's intervals between wetting grow longer and they show interest in the potty. Rather than a set age, it's important to watch for your child's signs of readiness and proceed without rushing.

Q. Can a potty training storybook help?

A. Seeing the hero of the story succeed on the potty and get praised gives your child courage. Reading a potty training storybook together eases the fear of the toilet and makes them want to try on their own.

Q. How should I respond to an accident?

A. Accidents are a natural part of the process, so reassure rather than scold. When you show big joy at a success, your child gradually gains confidence.
